clinicalPearls: A fibro-inflammatory plaque encasing the infrarenal aorta and iliac vessels that spreads to envelop the ureters, typically presenting with insidious back, flank or abdominal pain that is dull and poorly localised.
Ureteric entrapment causing progressive obstructive uropathy and hydronephrosis is the dominant complication; renal impairment may be the presenting feature and can be silent until advanced.
Classically periaortic tissue displaces the ureters medially, in contrast to malignant nodal disease which tends to displace them laterally, though this rule is imperfect.
A substantial subset is now recognised as part of the IgG4-related disease spectrum, with tissue plasma-cell infiltration, raised serum IgG4 and response to immunosuppression.
Inflammatory markers are frequently raised and constitutional symptoms such as malaise, low-grade fever and weight loss are common, supporting the systemic inflammatory nature.
Cross-sectional imaging shows a confluent soft-tissue rind around the aorta that characteristically does not lift the vessel off the vertebral bodies, unlike a bulky lymphoma mass.
Corticosteroids are the mainstay and often produce rapid symptomatic and radiological regression; steroid-sparing agents or tamoxifen are used for maintenance or relapse.
Always exclude a secondary cause — malignancy, drugs, infection, prior radiotherapy or aortic aneurysm — before labelling disease idiopathic.
reference.pathophysiology: Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis is a chronic non-suppurative fibro-inflammatory process centred on the abdominal aorta and iliac arteries, now conceptualised as one manifestation of chronic periaortitis. An initial insult, thought in many cases to be an exaggerated local immune-inflammatory reaction to oxidised lipid and ceroid within an atherosclerotic aortic wall, triggers a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate that extends into the surrounding retroperitoneal fat. Over time a dense, avascular, collagen-rich plaque forms and contracts, encasing and constricting adjacent tubular structures, most importantly the ureters, but also the great vessels, gonadal vessels and occasionally the duodenum or bile ducts. In a proportion of patients the infiltrate is dominated by IgG4-positive plasma cells with storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis, placing the disease within the IgG4-related disease family and often accompanied by fibrosis at other sites. The systemic features and raised acute-phase response reflect an underlying autoimmune or dysimmune predisposition, and associations with autoimmune conditions, HLA alleles and asbestos or tobacco exposure have been described. The clinical consequences arise from mechanical entrapment rather than tissue invasion, so fibrosis progresses centrifugally, sparing the tissue planes that malignancy would breach.
additionalDifferentials: Retroperitoneal lymphoma or metastatic nodal disease
Chronic infective process such as tuberculous or fungal retroperitonitis
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis to characterise the periaortic rind and ureteric involvement
Renal function and imaging for hydronephrosis with assessment of split renal function
Serum IgG4 and immunoglobulin subclasses with inflammatory markers
18F-FDG PET to assess metabolic activity, disease extent and treatment response
Image-guided or surgical biopsy where malignancy cannot be excluded or the presentation is atypical
Autoimmune screen including antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies
Ureteric stenting or nephrostomy with drainage studies when obstruction is present
redFlags: Rapidly deteriorating renal function or anuria suggesting bilateral ureteric obstruction or an obstructed solitary kidney
Features of aortic aneurysm expansion, dissection or limb ischaemia from vascular encasement
Systemic symptoms with a bulky or atypical mass raising concern for underlying malignancy
Lower-limb oedema or venous thrombosis from caval or iliac vein compression
Failure to regress or paradoxical progression despite adequate immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: With early corticosteroid therapy and relief of ureteric obstruction the prognosis is generally good and renal function often recovers, though relapse is common and prolonged maintenance therapy or surgical ureterolysis may be required. Delayed diagnosis with established obstructive nephropathy or an unrecognised malignant or aggressive vascular cause carries a substantially worse outlook.
pitfalls: Attributing the mass to idiopathic disease without excluding lymphoma, carcinoma or an infective cause by adequate biopsy when features are atypical.
Overlooking silent bilateral ureteric obstruction because pain is mild and creatinine rise is insidious.
Failing to recognise coexisting IgG4-related disease at other sites, which changes surveillance and treatment.
Assuming medial ureteric deviation is diagnostic when it can occur in malignancy and its absence does not exclude the disease.
Stopping immunosuppression too early and missing relapse, which frequently occurs as markers rebound.
